source: Silman, Complete Endgame Course, Part One: basic mates (K+Q vs K)
reference_explanation: King and Queen versus King is a basic, must-know mate. The lone King is driven to the edge of the board; the Queen confines it a knight's-move away while White's own King marches up to support the mate. The one thing to watch is stalemate: keep the enemy King with a legal move until the King arrives to deliver checkmate on the edge.
key_ideas: drive the king to the edge

source: Silman, Complete Endgame Course, Part One: basic mates (K+R vs K)
reference_explanation: King and Rook versus King wins by the 'box' method. The two Kings take the opposition while the Rook cuts the enemy King off along a rank or file, and the White King then forces the defender back one rank at a time until a rook check delivers mate along the edge. The Rook does the confining; the King does the pushing.
key_ideas: cut the king off with the rook

source: Silman, Complete Endgame Course, Class C: King and Pawn vs Lone King
reference_explanation: An extra pawn is not always enough to win. With the defending King planted in front of the pawn and holding the opposition, King and Pawn versus King is a draw: whenever the stronger King tries to advance, the defender mirrors it and takes the opposition back, so the King can never be dislodged from the queening path and the pawn can never break through.
key_ideas: defender in front of the pawn draws
extra pawn is not always a win

source: Silman, Complete Endgame Course, Class C: Entering the Square of the Pawn (book p.106)
reference_explanation: To judge whether a lone King can catch a passed pawn, picture the 'square' of the pawn — the box whose side runs from the pawn to its queening square. If the defending King cannot step into that square on its move, the pawn promotes by force with no help needed from its own King. Here Black's King lies well outside the square, so White simply runs the pawn with 1.a6 and queens.
key_ideas: king outside the square cannot catch it

source: Silman, Complete Endgame Course, Class C: King and Pawn vs Lone King (key squares)
reference_explanation: In King and pawn versus King the win turns on the opposition and the pawn's key squares. When the stronger King reaches the sixth rank in front of its pawn it has seized the key squares and wins no matter whose move it is. Here 1.Kd6 shoulders the black King aside and clears the way, so the pawn advances with the King escorting it to promotion.
key_ideas: king on the sixth rank ahead of the pawn wins

source: Silman, Complete Endgame Course, Class C: Bishop and Wrong Colored Rook-Pawn vs Lone King (book p.112)
reference_explanation: A rook-pawn with the 'wrong' Bishop — one that does not control the square on which the pawn promotes — is only a draw once the defending King reaches the queening corner. Sitting in the corner in front of the promotion square, the lone King simply cannot be driven out (any attempt is stalemate or lets it shuffle back), so here the extra pawn and Bishop are worthless and the game is drawn.

source: Silman, Complete Endgame Course, Class C: The Philidor Position (book p.126, diagram 130)
reference_explanation: White is a pawn up with a better King and a more active Rook, yet this Philidor Position is a dead draw. The defender keeps his Rook on the third rank in front of the pawn (here 1...Rh6) so the enemy King can never advance to the sixth rank. Only when White finally pushes the pawn to the sixth does the Rook drop to the rear and check the White King endlessly from behind. Learn this and you can hold the position against any grandmaster.
key_ideas: stop the king reaching the sixth
checks from the rear once the pawn advances

source: Silman, Complete Endgame Course, Class C: The Lucena Position (book p.121, diagram 125)
reference_explanation: The Lucena is the 'sacred key' to all rook endings: the stronger side has an extra pawn on the seventh rank with its own King in front of the pawn. To win, White must free his King from in front of the pawn and escort it to promotion. Because the black King and Rook stop the King escaping, White drives the black King away with 1.Rf2+!, gaining the tempo to bring the Rook to the fourth rank and 'build a bridge' that blocks the coming checks while the King steps out and the pawn queens.
key_ideas: extra pawn on the seventh with king in front
drive the enemy king away with a rook check
build a bridge on the fourth rank

source: Silman, Complete Endgame Course, Class C: Bishops of Opposite Colors (book p.120, diagram 124)
reference_explanation: With Bishops of opposite colors an extra pawn often means nothing. The passed pawn is blockaded on a square the defender's King can sit on forever, and the attacker's Bishop, running on the other color, can never influence that square or dislodge the King. The defender draws by keeping his King on the blockade square and his Bishop guarding its own pawns, shuffling harmlessly back and forth. When in trouble, trading into opposite-colored bishops is an excellent last-stand strategy.
key_ideas: wrong-color bishop cannot evict the king

source: Reti 1928 study (a staple of endgame courses): the king on two errands
reference_explanation: Reti's celebrated study shows the King doing two jobs at once. White looks lost — he cannot obviously catch Black's h-pawn and his own c-pawn seems too far advanced to be stopped — yet 1.Kg7! heads toward both errands simultaneously: the King steps into the square of the h-pawn while also hurrying to support the c-pawn's promotion. Thanks to the diagonal geometry of the board, whatever Black tries White arrives just in time, and the game is drawn.
key_ideas: enter the square of the pawn
